localNote: The four Wetherspoons in the Stoke-on-Trent area reflect the Potteries' industrial heritage. The Reginald Mitchell in Hanley honours the designer of the Spitfire and occupies a Grade II listed former meat market. The Wheatsheaf in Stoke is on the site of a coaching inn from 1818, while The Arnold Machin in Newcastle-under-Lyme sits in a former Post Office and The Bradley Green in Biddulph takes its name from the area's old coal-mining identity.

pubs.name: The Reginald Mitchell
pubs.history: Named after the Butt Lane-born aeronautical engineer who designed the Supermarine Spitfire. He was educated at Hanley High School. The Grade II listed building was originally Hanley's meat market and later served as a shopping centre.
pubs.nearestStation: Stoke-on-Trent station, about 10 minutes by bus

pubs.name: The Bradley Green
pubs.history: Named after the historical name for Biddulph during the nineteenth-century coal and iron boom. The town was called Bradley Green until 1930, when Biddulph appeared on Ordnance Survey maps. The building was formerly a Congleton Co-operative Society premises.
pubs.nearestStation: Congleton station, about 10 minutes by car

pubs.name: The Wheatsheaf
pubs.history: The site has been a local landmark since at least 1818, when it served as a coaching inn on the route between Newcastle-under-Lyme and Derby. The previous building was demolished in 1963. Before Wetherspoon took over in 1998, the venue was known as a live music pub.
pubs.nearestStation: Stoke-on-Trent station, about 5 minutes on foot

pubs.name: The Arnold Machin
pubs.history: Named after the Staffordshire-born sculptor Arnold Machin, who designed the portrait of Queen Elizabeth II used on British postage stamps since 1967. The pub occupies a former Post Office, a fitting link to his stamp design legacy.
pubs.nearestStation: Newcastle-under-Lyme has no station; Stoke-on-Trent station is about 15 minutes by bus
